title: Snowfall Totals Map (Season Archive) Explorer
description: Explore a full winter's snowfall totals around any point with the Snowfall Totals Map (Season Archive) — ERA5 weather-archive data, mapped. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, lake-effect country near Buffalo, New York averages roughly 95 inches (241 cm) of snow a season in published climate records — the kind of total this archive map lets you compare winter by winter.
quick_answer: The Snowfall Totals Map (Season Archive) maps the total snowfall for a winter season around your point, summed from the ERA5 weather archive rather than measured live. Pick a point and a season and read the totals cell by cell — last winter against the famous ones.

body.t: Was last winter really snowier, or just better timed? Season totals from one consistent archive settle the argument the way memory cannot.

Seasonal totals size contracts, roof-load expectations and salt budgets better than any single storm headline.
Lake-effect belts, elevation bands and rain-shadow edges all sign their names in season totals. The archive lets you read the signature.
Each cell sums the archive's daily snowfall from December 1 to March 31 for the chosen season, over a 5×5 grid spanning about 25 miles. A cell is a neighbourhood's winter, not one garden's.

Published climate averages put Syracuse, New York near 127 inches (323 cm) in a typical season — among the snowiest US cities — driven by Lake Ontario. Archive maps show the narrow bands that produce those averages.

popular_table.note: Reanalysis blends observations into a model grid (roughly 25–30 km cells), so a single valley or ridge can differ from its cell. Treat totals as regional truth, not fence-post truth.

faq: Which winters can I look up?
Any season the ERA5 archive covers — the reanalysis reaches back decades, so famous historical winters and last winter sit in the same dataset, computed the same way.
Why does my town's official total differ?

Official station totals are point measurements; archive cells are area averages from a model grid. Lake-effect bands and elevation can put a station well above or below its cell — both numbers are honest answers to different questions.
Snowfall versus snow depth — settled how?
The map totals new snowfall across the season. A place can receive 200 cm of snow and never hold more than 40 cm on the ground, because depth melts, settles and blows away between storms.
Does it include snow outside December to March?
The season window is fixed at December 1 to March 31, so October and April snow — real in northern and mountain country — is outside this map's totals.
How far back does the archive go?
ERA5 reanalysis extends back to 1940 in its current form, with the densest observation support in recent decades. Early seasons carry wider uncertainty.
Can I use this for a roof-load or insurance decision?
As background only. Design loads and claims use official station records and engineering standards — the archive is a comparison tool, not an authority.
Why is there snow in a cell over the ocean?
Lake and sea surfaces do receive snowfall in the model world, and coastal cells mix land and water. Read coastal cells as the blend they are.
